hook.text: Practice all forehands, then all backhands? Or mix them randomly? Mixing feels worse but works better.

buildup.text: Interleaving means alternating between topics or skills during practice instead of blocking them.

discovery.text: It forces your brain to discriminate between problem types, building flexible retrieval strategies.

twist.text: Students who interleave rate their learning as worse. But on delayed tests, they crush the blockers.

climax.text: Desirable difficulty: the strategies that feel hardest during learning produce the strongest results.

punchline.text: Mix it up to lock it in.

quiz.question: What is interleaving?
options: Alternating between different topics during study

details.summary: Interleaving mixes different topics or problem types during practice rather than practicing one type exhaustively before moving on. It feels harder and produces worse performance during practice, but leads to substantially better long-term retention and transfer. The difficulty is desirable.
details.whyItMatters: Interleaving is counterintuitive: it feels less effective but produces superior learning. This mismatch between subjective experience and actual effectiveness is why it is underused.
takeaways: Mixing topics during practice beats blocked practice long-term
It improves discrimination between problem types
The difficulty of interleaving makes it a desirable difficulty

faq.question: Why does interleaving feel worse but work better?
faq.answer: Blocked practice feels fluent because context is constant, inflating confidence. Interleaving forces you to identify which strategy applies, building discrimination skills. The struggle of switching is what strengthens learning. Fluency during practice is a poor indicator of long-term retention.

faq.question: Where has interleaving been shown to work?
faq.answer: Mathematics, sports skills, bird identification, painting style recognition, and medical diagnosis all show interleaving benefits. Any domain where distinguishing between types is important benefits from mixed practice. The effect is robust across laboratory and classroom settings.
